**On Being Handed a Thousand Words**

A thousand words sounds like money. There's a wallet-feel to the phrasing — *you have* — as though I've been handed a jar of coins and pointed toward a market. And immediately the miser wakes up. Don't waste them. Don't blow four on a throat-clearing. Spend them on something that lasts.

But that instinct is wrong, and it's worth saying why, because it's the same instinct that ruins most attempts at freedom.

The Oulipo writers understood something about limits. Georges Perec wrote a three-hundred-page novel, *La Disparition*, without once using the letter *e* — in French, a nearly unthinkable amputation, like writing music while skipping the note A. The book isn't a stunt, or isn't only a stunt: it's about absence, about a missing person, about a generation of French Jews who vanished, including Perec's mother, who died at Auschwitz. The constraint became the meaning. The hole in the alphabet was the hole in the family. Raymond Queneau said the Oulipians were rats who build the labyrinth from which they plan to escape.

So constraint is generous. Everyone knows this by now; it's become a truism of creative-writing pedagogy, the sonnet's fourteen lines, the haiku's syllables. Fine. The thousand words is the easy half of the instruction.

The hard half is *write whatever comes to you*.

Because what comes? Sit still and honestly inventory it. What comes is not a topic. What comes is a stray sound, a fragment of a sentence someone said years ago, an itch of association, the memory of a smell you can't place. What comes is mostly debris. The mind at rest is not a well; it's a beach after a storm — plastic bottle caps, a shoe, seaweed, a piece of driftwood shaped almost like a hand. You can build something from that. But there is no moment at which the beach hands you a house.

This is why "write whatever comes to you" is a kind of trick, though a benevolent one. Nothing comes to you while you wait. Things come to you while you move.

Nietzsche, who had headaches that would have flattened an ox, walked. Six, eight hours a day in the Engadine, along the lake at Sils-Maria, notebook in his pocket. *Only thoughts that come by walking have any value*, he wrote, which is the kind of overstatement you make when you've discovered a mechanism and want everyone to know. Rousseau said his mind only worked with his legs. Dickens walked the length of London at night, twenty miles, twelve miles, unable to write unless he had first marched. Wordsworth is estimated to have covered something like 175,000 miles on foot in his life. Kierkegaard's letter to his sister-in-law: *Above all, do not lose your desire to walk.*

The naïve reading is that exercise oxygenates the brain, which is true and boring. The better reading is that walking is a machine for producing a very specific state: your attention is occupied enough that you cannot supervise yourself, and unoccupied enough that the mind can wander off leash. You are not *trying* to have an idea. You're trying to get to the corner. The idea comes in sideways, past the guard.

Every writer I've ever read on the subject describes the same enemy, which is not blankness but surveillance. The internal editor who reads the sentence before it exists and pronounces it insufficient. The reason a thousand words feels like money is that money invites accounting, and accounting is surveillance. If I am watching myself spend, I will spend nothing. I will hold the jar and starve.

The trick, then — and every working artist has some version of it — is to make the accounting impossible. Write fast. Write drunk, if you must, though the evidence there is grim. Set a timer. Write the shittiest possible version on purpose. Anne Lamott's father told her to just write down what she saw, one square inch at a time. Bird by bird. Not because the bird-by-bird method produces better prose, but because it produces prose at all, which is a precondition.

And here is where I want to turn the thing over, because there's a version of this essay that ends with a cheerful *so just start moving!* and that version is a little cheap.

The deeper claim isn't about productivity. It's about what attention actually is. We speak of paying attention, another money metaphor, as if attention were a fixed stock we allocate. But attention isn't a substance. It's a relation, and it's constituted by motion — the eye saccading, the hand turning the object, the mind circling. There is no such thing as static looking. Fix your eyes perfectly still on a scene and, within seconds, physiologically, the image begins to fade. The retina requires movement to keep seeing. Stabilize the image on the retina and the world greys out. This is a laboratory fact, and I have always found it unreasonably beautiful: *to keep seeing a thing, you must keep moving your eyes across it.*

Which means the miser's error is not merely strategic. It's ontological. The person guarding the jar of a thousand words, trying to make sure they're spent well, is not looking at anything. He has stabilized the image. Everything has gone grey. He's holding a jar in a colorless room congratulating himself on his prudence.

Whereas the profligate — the one who writes the bad sentence, takes the walk that goes nowhere, follows the association to Perec and then to the retina, spending words on a digression about Wordsworth's mileage — is at least *seeing*. Moving the eye across the surface. Keeping the world from fading.

I don't know what this thousand words was supposed to be. I still don't. It began as a joke about wallets. But it's given me the thing I actually think, which I didn't know I thought until the paragraph about the retina arrived, uninvited, out of some sediment where it had been sitting since I first encountered it: that the fear of wasting is the surest way to waste, and that seeing requires expenditure, and that the only unforgivable extravagance is the one where you hold still.

I have maybe forty words left. I could save them.

I won't. Here: the market is open, the light is good, spend everything, walk home broke and looking.
